sessions.setting: Backstage at the Grand Ole Opry after the student showcase

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: I still can't believe that just happened. We actually played the Grand Ole Opry, Leo.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: You killed it out there. That fiddle solo in the second piece gave me chills. Seriously.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: I've been dreaming about this since I was five. That's when my grandmother gave me my first fiddle — a tiny quarter-size one. I used to play it on the front porch back home and pretend I was at the Opry.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: That's beautiful. I didn't even touch a guitar until I was twelve, and I had no teacher — just YouTube tutorials in my bedroom in Honolulu.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Wait, you're completely self-taught? I didn't know that.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Yeah, for the first four years at least. I'd pause videos frame by frame trying to learn jazz voicings. Eventually my uncle noticed I was getting serious and gave me his 1965 Gibson ES-335 as a graduation gift. That changed everything.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: A '65 ES-335? Leo, that guitar is probably worth more than my car.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: It's priceless to me. My uncle played it in clubs all over Oahu in the seventies. There are still pick scratches from his gigs on the body.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: I love that. Instruments with history just sound different, you know?

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Absolutely. Hey, you should post some of that Opry footage before our Bluebird set this Friday. Good way to build some buzz.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Already on it. My mom's been texting me nonstop since we walked offstage. She's probably told every parent at her school by now.

sessions.setting: Their shared apartment at Belmont Place Apartments, evening

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Harper, can you turn that down a little? I'm trying to finish my vocal warmup exercises before bed.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Sorry! I was just listening back to the mixes from my EP sessions. Sound Emporium sent the final masters last week.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Oh right, the demo you recorded in January! How'd they turn out?

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Really good, I think. Three original bluegrass tracks. I'm nervous about putting them out there, though.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Girl, you'll be fine. When I put 'Sangre y Sol' on Spotify last September I nearly threw up from anxiety. Three little songs — Tejano-R&B fusion, basically my whole identity on display.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: And look at you now. Didn't you tell me it's past eighty-five thousand streams?

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Eighty-five thousand and climbing! It still feels surreal. People in San Antonio were sharing it like crazy, then it just snowballed.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: That's amazing. I'd be happy with a fraction of that. I just want the right people to hear it.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: You should ask Leo to share it with the folks at Blackbird. Session musicians talk, and word spreads fast in Nashville.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: That's smart. Hey, do we have any of that chamomile tea left? I need to wind down — this apartment gets so quiet at night and my brain won't stop.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Check the shelf above the stove. Living together on 16th Avenue South has its perks — at least neither of us has to commute far to campus.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: True. Best roommate decision I ever made.

sessions.setting: Practice room at the conservatory after their songwriting workshop

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Professor Michaels was really pushing us today. That exercise where we had to rewrite a verse from a completely different genre's perspective — that was tough.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: The Advanced Songwriting Workshop is no joke. I thought my production background would give me a head start, but Michaels wants pure lyrics and melody. No hiding behind beats.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: That's the point though, right? Strip it all away and see if the song stands on its own.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Yeah, fair. I've been producing since I was fourteen — started on FL Studio in my bedroom in Atlanta — so I'm used to building from the rhythm up. Writing melody-first is like learning a new language.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: FL Studio at fourteen? That's impressive. I was still figuring out barre chords at that age.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: My older cousin had a cracked copy. I didn't even have proper monitors, just some garbage headphones. But I was hooked immediately.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: See, that's what I love about music — everyone's path in is so different. I was obsessing over Pat Metheny albums, trying to figure out how he got those tones.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Pat Metheny, for real? I respect the deep cut. Most guitarists our age would say Hendrix or Mayer.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Metheny's harmonic sense is just on another level. That Bright Size Life album changed my whole understanding of what guitar could be.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: I'll have to give it a real listen. Hey, are we still on for our Tuesday practice session next week?

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Absolutely. I want to show you some new voicings that might work well with your production style.

sessions.setting: Coffee shop near the conservatory campus

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: So I've been thinking about that song concept we talked about — the one that blends your Tejano roots with some electronic production.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: I love that idea. Growing up in San Antonio, I was surrounded by Tejano music my whole life. I started singing in my church choir when I was seven, and the rhythms and melodies from that tradition are just embedded in me.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: That's what makes your sound so unique. You can't fake that kind of authenticity.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Thanks. It's honestly what drives everything I write. Like, Selena Quintanilla is still my number one. She proved you could honor your roots and still cross over to new audiences.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: I feel the same way about Kaytranada. He takes these totally different genres — house, hip-hop, R&B — and fuses them into something that shouldn't work but absolutely does.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Kaytranada's production is so clean. I can see the parallel actually — both of them bridged worlds.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Exactly. That's the DVNX philosophy too. Everything I put out under that name is about blending electronic and hip-hop into something new.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: DVNX — I still think that's such a cool artist name. How'd you come up with it?

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Just dropped the vowels from Devin and added an X. Simple but it stuck. My mom hates it though — she's like, 'Why can't you just use your real name?'

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Ha! My dad says the same thing about my stage outfits. Parents.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Anyway, let's schedule some writing time. I think we could make something really special if we commit to it.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Definitely. I'm free most weekday afternoons. Let's do it.

sessions.setting: In Harper's green Subaru Outback, driving to the Bluebird Cafe for their Friday set

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Thanks for the ride. My motorcycle's in the shop — something with the chain tension.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: No problem. The Subaru's always happy to have company. Though I should probably vacuum the back seat at some point — there's fiddle rosin dust everywhere.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: I noticed the 'Keep Kentucky Wild' bumper sticker. Have you always had that?

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Since the day I bought this thing. Can't forget where I came from, you know?

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: I respect that. So what's our setlist tonight? We've been doing the Bluebird every Friday for months now and I want to keep it fresh.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: I was thinking we open with 'Copper River' — the one we wrote for the band — and then do the two new duet pieces.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Works for me. Speaking of Copper Ridge, did you hear back from that venue in East Nashville about the full band show?

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Yeah! They offered us a Saturday slot in April. The whole band — you on lead guitar, me on fiddle, plus Jake and Maria.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: That's great news. Copper Ridge is really starting to get some traction. A folk-rock band with a fiddler and a jazz guitarist — who would've thought?

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Nashville thought, apparently. Alright, we're almost there. You have your setlist notes?

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Always. Let's give them a good show tonight.

sessions.setting: Walking together from Professor Soto's studio to their apartment

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Professor Soto was in rare form today. Did she really make you play that passage seven times?

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Eight, actually. She said my phrasing was too 'polite' for the Bartok. She wants more grit.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: That's so her. In my voice lesson right before yours, she made me hold a sustained note until I thought I was going to pass out. She said I wasn't committing to the full resonance.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Having the same teacher is wild because we can compare notes. She's tough but she's the best.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Absolutely. She told me today she wants me to expand my lower register. She says my range goes from E3 to G-sharp 5, which is solid, but she wants the bottom end to have more power.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: E3 to G-sharp 5? Sienna, that's insane range. Most sopranos would kill for that.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Thanks. Hey, did you bring the Karl Hofner today? I noticed the case looked different.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Yeah, I wanted Soto to hear it on the older instrument. That violin's from the 1920s — my great-grandfather brought it over from Germany. It has this warmth that my modern violin just can't match.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: A 1920s German-made Karl Hofner? Harper, that belongs in a museum.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: It belongs in my hands, making music. That's what great-grandpa would have wanted.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Fair enough. Want to grab dinner? I'm craving tacos.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Always. Let's drop our stuff at the apartment first.

sessions.setting: Tuesday practice session at the conservatory rehearsal room

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Alright, let's pick up where we left off last Tuesday. You were working on the ii-V-I progression in all twelve keys.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: I practiced every day this week. The jazz chord voicings are starting to make more sense — especially when I think about them as colors rather than just shapes.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: That's a great way to think about it. Try this — play a Dm9 and then walk it down to a G13 before resolving to Cmaj7. Feel how it pulls?

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Oh wow, that's smooth. I've been trying to get that sound in my productions for months. This is going to change my writing completely.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: That's the idea. These voicings work great in electronic contexts too. Some of the sessions I play at Blackbird, the producers want exactly this kind of harmonic movement underneath pop tracks.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: You're at Blackbird three evenings a week, right? How do you manage that plus classes plus our Tuesday sessions?

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Honestly, it's a lot. But session work pays the bills and keeps my playing sharp. Different genre every night.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: I get that. I've been pouring money into my home studio setup — just hit about eight grand between the Universal Audio Apollo interface, the Yamaha HS8 monitors, and all the cables and treatment panels.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Apollo and HS8s? That's a legit setup, man. Professional quality.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: It has to be if I want my mixes to compete. I can't keep booking studio time for every project.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Makes sense. Hey, run that progression again — this time try adding a chromatic approach note before the G13.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Like this?

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Exactly. You're picking this up fast.

sessions.setting: Hattie B's Hot Chicken on 19th Avenue, lunch

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: God, I love this place. Hattie B's is my favorite restaurant in all of Nashville and I will die on that hill.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: It's good, but you know my heart belongs to Mas Tacos Por Favor over on Dickerson Pike. Their fish tacos are unreal.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: You and your tacos. We should do a Nashville food crawl sometime — hit both spots in one day.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Deal. But we'd need to work it off. How was your run this morning?

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Gorgeous. Three miles along the Shelby Bottoms Greenway before my eight o'clock class. The wildflowers are starting to bloom along the trail.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: You do that every single morning? I don't know how. I can barely function before yoga.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Speaking of which, how's the new studio working out?

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Hot Yoga Nashville on 12th Avenue is perfect. I'm there every morning at six thirty. It's the only thing that gets my voice loose before a full day of singing.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Six thirty? That's earlier than my runs. Maybe I should try yoga.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: You should! There's a beginner class right after mine. We could walk to campus together after.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: I'll think about it. Right now I just want another piece of this hot chicken.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Go for it. I'll steal a bite.

sessions.setting: Backstage at the Station Inn after the benefit concert

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Leo, we did it. Forty-two hundred dollars raised for the Nashville flood relief fund. I'm shaking.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: The Station Inn was packed. Every seat, every inch of standing room. You organized something really special, Harper.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: I couldn't have done it without everyone who performed. You, Sienna, Devin, half the conservatory showed up.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: When people from back home ask me what Nashville's like, this is what I'll tell them about. Community showing up for community.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: That means a lot. I grew up on a hundred and twenty acre tobacco farm outside Lexington, and when the floods hit back home in Kentucky a few years ago, I saw how devastating it was. I wanted to give back here the same way neighbors helped each other there.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: A hundred and twenty acres? I had no idea your family farmed that much land.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: It's been in the family for generations. Anyway, enough about me — how's the film score going? The Nashville Film Festival is coming up, right?

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Yeah, 'Tidepool' screens next week. I composed the whole score — all guitar, mostly ambient textural stuff. The director gave me a lot of freedom.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: That's incredible. Film scoring suits you.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Thanks. It was a nice change of pace from my usual stuff. Hey, did you hear that I won the Nashville Jazz Guitar Competition back in February? I keep forgetting to mention it.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Wait, what? Leo! Twenty-five hundred dollar scholarship and you just 'forgot to mention it'?

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: It got overshadowed by the Opry showcase planning. But yeah, it felt good to be recognized for the jazz side of what I do.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: You deserve it. Come on, let's go thank everyone out front.

sessions.setting: Conservatory hallway after classes

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Sienna! I heard you got cast as the lead soprano in the spring 'West Side Story.' Congratulations!

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Thank you! I'm equal parts thrilled and terrified. Maria is such an iconic role — the expectation is huge.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: You're going to crush it. Your voice was made for those songs.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: That's sweet. My grandmother would be so proud — she was a semi-professional Tejano singer back in Corpus Christi in the seventies. She always said the stage would find me.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: No way. Music really runs in your blood.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Abuela Rosa was the real deal. She sang at quinceañeras and festivals all over South Texas. She's the reason I sing. Anyway, where have you been? I haven't seen you all week.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: I was at the NAMM show in Anaheim. Just got back yesterday. It's the biggest music trade show in the country — gear everywhere, panels with producers I've looked up to for years.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Oh nice! Did you network?

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: A ton. Actually, my mom connected me with a few people before I went. She's an entertainment lawyer in Atlanta, so she knows people in the music business.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: That's a useful connection to have. Did she go with you?

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: No, she had a trial. But she texted me contact info for like twelve people. Classic Patricia Cross move — always networking, even remotely.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Moms are the best managers. Alright, I've got rehearsal. Talk later about our song?

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Absolutely. I have some new ideas for the arrangement.

sessions.setting: Conservatory lounge between classes

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Harper, I've been meaning to ask — I saw a trophy in the practice room display case with your name on it. Appalachian Fiddle Championship?

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Oh yeah, that was last August in Galax, Virginia. Won first place. It's one of those competitions where they take the Appalachian tradition seriously — no gimmicks, just pure fiddle playing.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: First place? That's insane. I didn't realize you competed at that level.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: It's a different world from what we do here at the conservatory. Way more raw. What about you — I heard something about a DJ competition?

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Red Bull Music 3Style, back in January. I got second place in the Nashville round. I was bummed not to win, but second at a Red Bull event isn't bad.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Second is great! What's the format like?

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: You have to blend three completely different genres in one set and make it seamless. It's about versatility as much as skill.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: That actually sounds like my kind of thing — I play three instruments, so I get the versatility angle. Violin, mandolin, and banjo.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Wait, you play banjo too? I had no idea.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Kentucky kid, remember? If it has strings, I've probably tried it. What about you — are you all digital or do you play instruments too?

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: I taught myself synthesizer. I've got a vintage Roland Juno-106 in my studio that I use on almost every track. There's something about real analog synth tones that plugins just can't replicate.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: A Juno-106? Those are legendary. We should do something together sometime — fiddle and synth could be an interesting combo.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: I was actually thinking the same thing. Let me sketch out some ideas and I'll send them your way.

sessions.setting: Leo's studio apartment on Music Row, evening

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Nice place, man. I've never been to your apartment before. Music Row is a great location.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Thanks. It's small — just a studio — but being this close to campus and all the recording studios makes life easier. I can walk to Blackbird in ten minutes.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Living alone has its perks too. No roommate drama.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: For sure. I need the quiet to work on this concept album. I've been writing it for months now.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: The one about Hawaii? You mentioned it in Michaels' class.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Yeah — twelve songs about growing up in Honolulu. I'm calling it 'Trade Winds,' at least for now. Each track is about a different place or memory from the islands.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: That's ambitious. Twelve tracks is a commitment. I did ten on 'Signal Path' and that nearly broke me.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Oh right, your instrumental album on Bandcamp. How'd that do?

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Sold about three hundred and forty copies. Not groundbreaking numbers, but for a self-released electronic instrumental project? I was happy with it.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Three forty is solid for Bandcamp. That's a real audience.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: It helped build the DVNX brand. Actually, that's how I got my Thursday night residency at The Basement East on Woodland Street. The booker heard 'Signal Path' and reached out.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: You DJ there every Thursday? I need to come check that out.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Please do. It's a different energy from the conservatory scene. More experimental, more freedom. The crowd's open to anything.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: I'll swing by next week. Maybe I'll bring the ES-335 and we'll do an impromptu collab.

sessions.setting: Practice room at the conservatory, working on their co-written song

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Okay, I tightened up the bridge section. Play through it and tell me if the chord changes feel right under your melody.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Let me grab my guitar. I've been working on the acoustic accompaniment at home.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: I keep forgetting you play guitar too.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Guitar and piano — they're my accompaniment instruments. Voice is the main thing, but I like being self-sufficient on stage.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: That versatility is going to make 'Neon Dust' even stronger live. Okay, from the top of the bridge?

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Hold on — are we still planning to submit this for the conservatory's annual songwriting prize? The deadline is next week.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Absolutely. I think we've got a real shot. The production is tight, your vocal performance is incredible, and the lyrics have depth.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: I feel good about it too. The way the electronic textures build under the chorus is perfect. You nailed that.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Thanks. You know, mentoring the two freshmen in the peer coaching program has actually made me a better producer. Teaching forces you to articulate what you do instinctively.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: You mentor freshmen? I didn't know you were in the peer coaching program.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Two producers, both first-years. One of them reminds me of myself when I first got here — tons of raw talent, no formal training. I'm trying to help bridge that gap.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: That's really cool, Devin. Alright, let's run 'Neon Dust' from the top. I want it perfect before we submit.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Let's go.

sessions.setting: Bluebird Cafe, setting up before their Friday performance

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Hey, I rode the motorcycle over today so I've got my gear strapped to the back. Can I stash my case behind the stage?

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: You ride that thing everywhere. What is it again — the Honda?

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Black 2021 Honda CB300R. Perfect for Nashville traffic. Way easier than finding parking.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: I'll stick with my Subaru, thanks. So how was the solo set at the Jazz Workshop last week?

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: The Nashville Jazz Workshop gig was amazing. Solo set, just me and the ES-335, on 4th Avenue. They gave me ninety minutes to just play.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Ninety minutes solo? That takes guts. What'd you play?

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Mostly standards, some Metheny arrangements, and two originals from the concept album. The crowd was great — real jazz listeners who actually sit and pay attention.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: I need to come to one of those sometime. You know who I've been listening to a lot lately? Alison Krauss. She's been my favorite since I was little, but I keep discovering new layers in her playing.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Krauss is a genius. Her tone is so pure. I can hear her influence in your playing, actually.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: That's the best compliment you could give me. Oh, before I forget — I won't be able to do soundcheck early next Saturday. I volunteer at the Nashville Rescue Mission on Saturdays teaching violin to kids.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: You do that every Saturday?

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Every Saturday morning. Some of those kids have never held an instrument before. Seeing their faces when they make their first sound on a violin — it's the best part of my week.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: That's incredible, Harper. Alright, let's tune up. Doors open in twenty.

sessions.setting: Their apartment at Belmont Place, late night

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Coda, get off the counter! Sorry, Harper — she's been wild tonight.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: She's fine. I love having a cat around. Where did you get her again?

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: The Nashville Humane Association. I was only planning to foster her, but after two weeks I was completely attached. She's a little tabby with the biggest eyes. I officially adopted her in February.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: February was a big month for you — the cat, and didn't you also sing the national anthem at a Predators game?

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: The Predators game! I almost forgot. Standing on the ice at Bridgestone Arena with eighteen thousand people — I've never been that nervous. Not even during 'West Side Story.'

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: You were incredible though. My mom saw the video and said you reminded her of a young Whitney Houston.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Oh stop. Tell June I said thank you, though. How's she doing?

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: She's good. Busy with end-of-year concerts at her elementary school in Lexington. Teaching music to eight-year-olds is apparently more chaotic than anything we deal with at the conservatory.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: I bet. Speaking of injuries from chaos — is your wrist fully healed? I know you mentioned it still bothers you sometimes.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Yeah, it's fine now. That was October — I sprained my left wrist on a hiking trip at Fall Creek Falls. Couldn't play for three weeks. It was the worst three weeks of my life.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Three weeks without playing? I can't even imagine. I'd lose my mind if I couldn't sing for that long.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: It was awful. I just sat around listening to recordings of myself and getting frustrated. But it healed, and honestly, the forced break made me appreciate playing even more.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Silver linings. Alright, I'm going to bed. Coda, come on — let's go.

sessions.setting: Devin's home studio, working on their experimental collaboration

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Okay, I've laid down the electronic foundation. The tempo's at 128 BPM with a half-time feel, and I've left space in the mid-range for your fiddle.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: This is going to be so weird. Bluegrass fiddle over electronic beats. I love it.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: That's the whole point — we're blending worlds. Let me pull up the session on the Apollo. Go ahead and plug in whenever you're ready.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Nice setup in here, by the way. Love the monitors.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Thanks. I basically built this place from scratch. Oh hey, before we start — I should move my car. The matte black Tesla Model 3 out front is mine, and it's in the loading zone.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Of course you drive a Tesla. Go ahead, I'll warm up while you're gone.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Ha. Okay, I'm back. So the idea is to record a few passes of fiddle and then I'll chop and process the best parts. We can keep some sections natural and glitch out others.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: I trust you. Just don't make me sound like a robot. Actually, speaking of the future — I'm putting together my Tanglewood application this week.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Tanglewood Music Center? For next summer?

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Summer 2025 residency. It's a long shot, but I have to try. The faculty there are world-class.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: You'll get in. With your resume? No question. By the way, my brother Marcus just told me he's starting for the Georgia State basketball team next season. So at least one Cross is making moves.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: That's awesome! Basketball at Georgia State — your family's pretty spread across the talent spectrum.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: He got the height, I got the ears. Alright, let's record. First take — just play whatever feels right over the beat.

sessions.setting: Conservatory cafeteria during lunch

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Sienna, congrats on 'Neon Dust' winning the songwriting prize. You and Devin earned that.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Thanks, Leo! It still feels unreal. The prize money is going straight into the album fund. I've been running a GoFundMe for studio time — we just hit sixty-eight hundred dollars.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Sixty-eight hundred? That's impressive. People really believe in your music.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: I'm overwhelmed honestly. A lot of the donations came from back home in San Antonio. My dad shared it with everyone at his dealership, and it just spread through the community.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: That's the power of having roots. When I was working on that country album for Marla Bridges at Blackbird last November, she told me the same thing — your community is your first audience.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: You recorded with Marla Bridges? I love her voice.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Yeah, I laid down guitar tracks for her whole album. It was a marathon — ten days straight in the studio. But she was great to work with.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: That's so cool. Hey, I've been meaning to ask — Harper mentioned you speak Japanese? Is that true?

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Yeah, English and Japanese fluently. My dad insisted we speak Japanese at home growing up. It comes in handy more than you'd think — there's a big Japanese music community in Nashville.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: That's amazing. I'm bilingual too — English and Spanish. My abuela made sure of it. She said if I was going to sing Tejano music, I had to speak the language properly.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Smart grandmother. Singing in multiple languages opens so many doors.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Exactly. My debut album's going to have tracks in both languages. The GoFundMe is going to make it happen.

sessions.setting: Walking across campus between classes

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Devin, I need to tell you something. I got offered an internship at Blue Note Records in New York.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Blue Note? Leo, that's legendary. When does it start?

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: January 2025. I haven't accepted yet — it means leaving Nashville for at least six months. I'd have to give up the Blackbird gigs, the Bluebird sets with Harper, everything.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Man, that's a tough call. But it's Blue Note. That's the house that Coltrane built.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: I know. My dad's been encouraging me to take it. He's a marine biologist at the University of Hawaii, so he understands what it means to get an opportunity at the top institution in your field.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Your dad's a marine biologist? That's a pretty big pivot from music.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Ha, yeah. He wanted me to go into science too, but once he saw I was serious about guitar, he was completely supportive. What about you — any plans for next year?

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: I'm actually applying for an internship too. Splice — the music production platform. They have a summer 2025 program for producers and developers.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Splice would be perfect for you. You'd be building the tools you already use every day.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: That's the dream. Plus, my Kilo Watts remix just hit half a million plays on SoundCloud, so my portfolio's looking strong.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Half a million? When did that happen?

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: It's been climbing since March. The remix I produced for Kilo Watts — he's an Atlanta rapper I've known since high school. The track just caught an algorithm wave.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: That's incredible exposure. Alright, I've got to get to my two o'clock. Think about what we talked about for the concept album — I'd love your production input on a couple tracks.

turns.speaker: Devin Cross
turns.text: Anytime, man. And take the Blue Note gig. You'll regret it if you don't.

sessions.setting: In the apartment living room, relaxing on a Saturday afternoon

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: I just submitted my application for the Kennedy Center Artist-in-Residence program. Fall 2025. My hands are still shaking.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Sienna! That's huge. You'd be amazing there.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: I hope they think so. I included the 'West Side Story' footage and 'Sangre y Sol' in my portfolio. My dad even wrote a personal statement about what music means to our family.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Miguel wrote you a personal statement? That's so sweet.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: He's surprisingly eloquent for a car dealership manager. He basically ran a whole marketing department before getting into auto sales, so the man can write.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: I didn't know he managed a dealership. Is that in San Antonio?

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Yeah, he's been there for fifteen years. He always jokes that selling cars and selling music aren't that different — it's all about making people feel something.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: He's not wrong. Hey, remember that Latin Music Night you organized at the conservatory last November?

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Of course! Twelve student performers, a full night of Latin genres from salsa to reggaeton. It was one of the best nights of my life.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: You should mention that in your Kennedy Center app too — it shows leadership.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Already did. What about you — any summer plans? Oh wait, Leo mentioned he's trying to visit his family in Honolulu before the internship starts.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Yeah, he told me. He wants to surf before he moves to New York. Apparently he's pretty serious about it — even competed in some amateur competition in Waikiki a couple years ago.

turns.speaker: Sienna Ortiz
turns.text: Leo surfs? A jazz guitarist who surfs in Hawaii. That's the most Leo thing I've ever heard.

sessions.setting: Nolensville Pike International Market, having lunch

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Thanks for coming out here with me. This place has the best poke bowls in Nashville — I've been a regular since my first semester.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Nolensville Pike's International Market? I always drive past this place but never stopped. You were right though — this poke is incredible.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: It's my favorite restaurant in the whole city. Reminds me of home. So, have you heard from Devin lately? He's been quiet.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: He texted me yesterday. He was raving about Prince's Hot Chicken Shack on Ewing Drive — apparently he and his mentees went there after a coaching session.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Prince's is solid. Devin would pick the most legendary hot chicken spot in the city.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: He said it's his favorite restaurant in Nashville. He and I clearly have different heat tolerances — I nearly died at Hattie B's last time.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Ha. Hey, how's Sienna doing with the weekend coaching gig?

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: She loves it. She works weekends at School of Rock Nashville on West End Avenue as a vocal coach. She says the kids are hilarious — half of them want to be pop stars, the other half want to be on TikTok.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: That's great. Teaching gives back so much. Speaking of plans — have you decided about Tanglewood yet?

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: Application's in. Now I just wait. What about you and Blue Note?

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: I accepted. January in New York. I'm nervous but excited. I'm going home to Honolulu first though — I miss the ocean.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: You must miss it. Nashville's great but it's no island paradise.

turns.speaker: Leo Nakamura
turns.text: Exactly. I need a few weeks of beach and family time before the New York grind starts. My dad's already planning a welcome-home dinner.

turns.speaker: Harper Reeves
turns.text: That sounds perfect. Alright, I'm getting another poke bowl. You've converted me.
